**The Everything Drawer**

Every kitchen has one. Not a drawer with a purpose, but a drawer that absorbed one, the way an old coat absorbs smells. It is usually third from the top, near the phone charger, and it does not open so much as give. You have to lift the front slightly and coax it, because somewhere inside a twist tie has wedged itself against the runners, and the drawer has learned to live with compromise.

Open it. Go on. What do you find?

Rubber bands, gone brittle, some fused into a single archaeological layer. Batteries of unknown charge, which you keep because testing them requires a device that is also in the drawer. Keys to locks that no longer exist: the bicycle lock whose bicycle was stolen in 2011, kept on the theory that the bicycle might return; the key to a roommate's bedroom from a decade and three cities ago. A birthday candle shaped like a 6 that, with a match and some optimism, becomes a 9. Soy sauce packets, breeding. A single chopstick. The screw — there is always one screw — that fits nothing in the house, that came from nowhere, that cannot be thrown away because it might, somewhere, be load-bearing. The instruction manual for an appliance you no longer own, kept in case the appliance's ghost needs troubleshooting. A corkscrew, though you own a proper one, because the drawer's corkscrew is for emergencies, and emergencies, in the drawer's cosmology, are always wine-related. A pen that works — which is to say, the pen. The only pen in the house that has ever worked. Everyone knows it. No one says it. God help you if you try to take it to another room.

And the little flat screwdriver. Of course. The little flat screwdriver that has opened every paint can, every battery compartment, every stubborn childproof lid; the true sovereign of the household, though it has never once been put back where it belongs.

Why do these things end up here? Not laziness — or not only. The drawer is where intention goes to pause. Every item in it was, at some moment, on its way somewhere else. The key was going to be labeled. The battery was going to be tested. The screw was going to be returned to its machine, wherever that machine is. But putting something away requires a destination, and when the mind hesitates — *where does this belong?* — the hand, which cannot hover forever, chooses the drawer. It is the household's waiting room. Nothing is stored there. Things are parked.

This is why the drawer, alone in the house, tells the truth. Consider the rest of the kitchen: it performs. The good plates face forward. The spices are alphabetized by someone who once read an article about alphabetizing spices. The refrigerator door curates a family — the report cards, the vacation magnet, the photo where everyone is squinting and happy — a family that exists, certainly, but in a particular light. Even the junk mail on the counter is arranged to say: *we are people who will deal with this.*

The drawer performs nothing. The drawer is the household's unconscious. It is where a family keeps what it cannot use and cannot release. You want to know who people actually are? Don't read their bookshelves; bookshelves are aspirational. Open the drawer. There is the museum ticket from the rain day. The spare button from a coat that outlived its buttons. The birthday candles — meaning someone, once, turned six, or nine. The foreign coin — meaning someone went somewhere, or meant to. It is an autobiography written by accident, in no particular order, and therefore accurate.

I think about this when I hear about the children of someone who has died, tasked with clearing the house. The will disposes of the big things easily: the house, the car, the watch. But then there is a pause in the emptying-out, and someone opens the drawer. And this — not the jewelry, not the deeds — is where the grief actually lives. Because here are the dead person's hesitations, made physical. Here is what they couldn't part with and didn't need: the rubber band ball they were surely going to use. The key to something. Which thing? No one knows now. The question is unanswerable, so the key goes into an envelope, the envelope goes into a box, and the box goes to the new house, into a drawer.

We are, all of us, curators of a drawer we did not start and cannot end. Your mother had one. Her mother had one. Somewhere in your drawer is an item that migrated from theirs — a thimble, a strange magnet, a screw of great age — an heirloom so humble it can only be inherited by drawer.

And yet: faith. Because one day — not soon, the drawer is patient — the thing will break. The glasses will loosen at the hinge. The toy will need its battery door pried. The paint can, bought in a hurry for a wall you have stared at for six years, will sit unopened on the spread newspaper, and you will be standing there, and then you will remember. You will walk to the kitchen. You will lift the front of the drawer and coax it past the wedged twist tie. And there, beneath the soy sauce, gleaming like a relic: the little flat screwdriver, waiting all this time, keeping its one small promise.

Nothing is ever really lost in a house. It is only in the drawer.

**The Everything Drawer**

Every kitchen has one. Not a drawer with a purpose, but a drawer that absorbed one, the way an old coat absorbs smells. It is usually third from the top, near the phone charger, and it does not open so much as give. You have to lift the front slightly and coax it, because somewhere inside, a twist tie has wedged itself against the runners, and the drawer has learned to live with compromise.

Open it. Go on. What do you find?

Rubber bands, gone brittle, some fused into a single archaeological layer. Batteries of unknown charge, which you keep because testing them requires a device that is also in the drawer. Keys to locks that no longer exist: the bicycle lock whose bicycle was stolen in 2011, kept on the theory that the bicycle might return; the key to a roommate's bedroom from a decade and three cities ago. A birthday candle shaped like a 6 that, with a match and some optimism, becomes a 9. Soy sauce packets, breeding. A single chopstick. The screw — there is always one screw — that fits nothing in the house, that came from nowhere, that cannot be thrown away because it might, somewhere, be load-bearing. The instruction manual for an appliance you no longer own, kept in case the appliance's ghost needs troubleshooting. A corkscrew, though you own a proper one, because the drawer's corkscrew is for emergencies, and emergencies, in the drawer's cosmology, are always wine-related. A pen that works, which is to say: the pen. The only pen in the house that has ever worked, and everyone knows it, and no one says it, and God help you if you try to take it to another room.

And the little flat screwdriver. Of course. The little flat screwdriver that has opened every paint can, every battery compartment, every stubborn child-proof lid, that is the true sovereign of the household though it has never once been put back where it belongs.

Why do these things end up here? Not laziness, or not only. The drawer is where intention goes to pause. Every item in it was, at some moment, on its way somewhere else. The key was going to be labeled. The battery was going to be tested. The screw was going to be returned to its machine, wherever that machine is. But the moment of putting-away requires a destination, and when the mind hesitates — where does this belong? — the hand, which cannot hover forever, chooses the drawer. It is the household's waiting room. Nothing is stored there; things are parked.

And this is why the drawer, alone in the house, tells the truth. Consider the rest of the kitchen: it performs. The good plates face forward. The spices are alphabetized by someone who once read an article about alphabetizing spices. The refrigerator door curates a family — the report cards, the vacation magnet, the photo where everyone is squinting and happy — a family that exists, sure, but in a particular light. Even the junk mail on the counter is arranged to say: we are people who will deal with this.

The drawer performs nothing. The drawer is the household's unconscious. It is where the family keeps what it cannot use and cannot release. You want to know who people actually are? Don't read their bookshelves — bookshelves are aspirational. Open the drawer. There is the museum ticket from the rain day. The spare button from a coat that outlived its buttons. The birthday candles, meaning someone, once, turned six, or nine. The foreign coin, meaning someone went somewhere, or meant to. It is an autobiography written by accident, in no particular order, and therefore accurate.

I think about this when I hear about the children of someone who has died, tasked with clearing the house. The will disposes of the big things easily: the house, the car, the watch. But then there is a pause in the emptying-out, and someone opens the drawer. And this — not the jewelry, not the deeds — is where the grief actually lives. Because here is the dead person's hesitations, made physical. Here is what they couldn't part with and didn't need: the rubber band ball they were surely going to use. The key to something. Which thing? No one knows now. The question is unanswerable, and so the key goes into an envelope, and the envelope goes into a box, and the box goes to the new house, into a drawer.

We are, all of us, curators of a drawer we did not start and cannot end. Your mother had one. Her mother had one. Somewhere in your drawer is an item that migrated from theirs — a thimble, a strange magnet, a screw of great age — an heirloom so humble it can only be inherited by drawer.

And yet: faith. Because one day — not soon, the drawer is patient — the thing will break. The glasses will loosen at the hinge. The toy will need its battery door pried. The paint can, bought in a hurry for a wall you've stared at for six years, will sit unopened on the newspaper, and you'll be standing there, and then you'll remember. You'll walk to the kitchen. You'll lift the front of the drawer slightly and coax it past the wedged twist tie. And there, under the soy sauce, gleaming like a relic: the little flat screwdriver, waiting all this time, keeping its one small promise.

Nothing is ever really lost in a house. It is only in the drawer.
